title: Cloudsplitter Rockshelter (Menifee County)
summary: In the Red River Gorge sandstone country, Cloudsplitter Rockshelter holds a deep Archaic-to-Early Woodland record. Dry sand preserved a roughly 3,700-year-old squash rind—early…
bodyMarkdown:
Cloudsplitter Rockshelter is a sandstone overhang in Menifee County. Its dry deposits hold one of the longest records of human life in eastern Kentucky. They also hold some of the earliest evidence of plant gardening in eastern North America.

## Excavation

Earlier digs in eastern Kentucky rockshelters, during the 1920s and 1930s, had already pointed to early plant cultivation. But those excavations were not precise enough to answer many questions. That changed in 1978, when the National Science Foundation [funded excavations at Cloudsplitter](https://www.fs.usda.gov/ne/newtown_square/publications/technical_reports/pdfs/2000/274%20papers/ison274.pdf). One goal was to learn how people, especially early gardeners, changed the local environment.

The work produced the first widely recognized quantitative data on the shift toward horticulture in the eastern woodlands.

## Nine thousand years

The shelter's layers record about 9,000 years of human use. When people first camped there, around 7,000 B.C., the land was still recovering from the Ice Age. A dense stand of hemlock grew at the shelter then.

By about 1,000 B.C., in the Late Archaic period, the plant remains show a change. Seeds typical of forest edges suggest that people had cleared parts of the forest. Researchers think the cultivated plants found in those layers probably came from garden plots in those clearings.

## Early crops

The Late Archaic deposits contained squash, gourd, sunflower and goosefoot. A fragment of squash rind [about 3,700 years old](https://grokipedia.com/page/Red_River_Gorge) is among the best-known finds.

Goosefoot, or chenopod, is especially important. Accelerator dating of desiccated domesticated goosefoot seeds produced an age of [about 3,450 years before present](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/american-antiquity/article/abs/domesticated-chenopodium-in-prehistoric-eastern-north-america-new-accelerator-dates-from-eastern-kentucky/B3DF657F64BE25778F511C7C225E366B) at Cloudsplitter and about 3,400 at [Newt Kash](/stories/newt-kash-hollow-15mf1/). Those dates pushed back the known age of the domesticated plant by about 1,000 years.

## Kentucky today

Cloudsplitter and Newt Kash are central to the study of plant domestication in eastern North America. Later Woodland-era layers at other eastern Kentucky shelters add pottery, cordage, textiles and storage pits. These [later finds](https://grokipedia.com/page/Red_River_Gorge) show people continuing to use the shelters for thousands of years. Looting remains a serious threat to rockshelter sites.

One shelter in Lee County was severely vandalized before salvage excavations there in 1984. At Cloudsplitter, the 1978 excavation remains the basis for a record of about 9,000 years of human use and early gardening.
